title: What is `union()` vs `unionByName()` in Spark — `union` matches columns by position (breaks if order differs), `unionByName` matches by column name (safe even if order differs, supports `allowMissingColumns=True` in Spark 3.1+) — and why should you always prefer `unionByName`?

s1_definition.profdef: `union` stacks two DataFrames on top of each other by matching columns strictly by position, so the first column of one is combined with the first column of the other regardless of their names, which silently produces wrong data if the two schemas have the same columns in a different order. `unionByName` matches columns by name instead of position, so it lines up columns correctly even if the order differs, and with `allowMissingColumns=True` it tolerates one side missing some columns by filling them with nulls. You prefer `unionByName` because it is robust against column-order differences and schema drift that would otherwise corrupt data.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India merging two stacks of account forms into one big pile. `union` is like a careless clerk who assumes both stacks have the fields in the exact same order, so he copies the first box of form A into the first box of form B, the second into the second, and so on. If stack B happens to list the balance before the name while stack A lists the name before the balance, the clerk cheerfully writes customer names into the balance field and rupee amounts into the name field, and nobody notices until the numbers are nonsense. `unionByName` is the careful clerk who reads the field labels and puts the balance under balance and the name under name, no matter what order the fields appear in.
s1_definition.oneliner: `union` lines up columns by position and silently corrupts data when orders differ, while `unionByName` lines them up by name and is the safe default.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `union` stacks two DataFrames on top of each other by matching columns strictly by position, so the first column of one is combined with the first column of the other regardless of their names, which silently produces wrong data if the two schemas have the same columns in a different order. `unionByName` matches columns by name instead of position, so it lines up columns correctly even if the order differs, and with `allowMissingColumns=True` it tolerates one side missing some columns by filling them with nulls. You prefer `unionByName` because it is robust against column-order differences and schema drift that would otherwise corrupt data.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India merging two stacks of account forms into one big pile. `union` is like a careless clerk who assumes both stacks have the fields in the exact same order, so he copies the first box of form A into the first box of form B, the second into the second, and so on. If stack B happens to list the balance before the name while stack A lists the name before the balance, the clerk cheerfully writes customer names into the balance field and rupee amounts into the name field, and nobody notices until the numbers are nonsense. `unionByName` is the careful clerk who reads the field labels and puts the balance under balance and the name under name, no matter what order the fields appear in.

**One line to remember:** `union` lines up columns by position and silently corrupts data when orders differ, while `unionByName` lines them up by name and is the safe default.

sections.s2_technical:
Both operations combine two DataFrames into one with all the rows of both, like a SQL UNION ALL, so they do not remove duplicates. The difference is how columns are aligned. `df1.union(df2)` aligns purely by position: column one of df1 goes with column one of df2, and so on. It only checks that both have the same number of columns, not that the names or meanings match. So if df1 has columns in the order account id, holder name, balance, and df2 was built with holder name, account id, balance, then `union` will put df2's holder names under df1's account id column and df2's account ids under df1's holder name column. The schema looks fine and no error is thrown, but the data is scrambled, which is one of the nastiest silent bugs in Spark because it passes every type check if the types happen to line up.

`df1.unionByName(df2)` aligns by column name. It finds the column named account id in both and stacks them together, the same for holder name and balance, regardless of the physical order. This is why it is safe against reordering: it does the matching you actually meant. In Spark three point one and later, `unionByName` also accepts `allowMissingColumns=True`, which lets the two DataFrames have slightly different column sets; the result is the union of all columns, and wherever a side lacks a column its rows get null for that column. For example combining a legacy trades DataFrame that has no settlement date with a new one that does, `df_old.unionByName(df_new, allowMissingColumns=True)` produces one DataFrame where the old rows have null settlement date rather than failing.

The reason to always prefer `unionByName` is correctness and resilience. Pipelines evolve: upstream teams add columns, reorder selects, or build DataFrames through different code paths, and any of these can change column order without changing names. With `union`, such a harmless-looking change silently misaligns data and corrupts every downstream result. With `unionByName`, the same change just works because names are stable identifiers while positions are not. A senior-level nuance is that `unionByName` still requires the matched columns to have compatible types, and without the allow-missing flag it still fails if the column sets differ, which is actually desirable because it surfaces a real schema mismatch rather than hiding it. Another nuance is that even with `unionByName` you should be deliberate about nullability and type widening, and in production I often explicitly select a canonical column order with `select` before unioning so the intent is visible in the code, but the matching itself should always be by name. The only time plain `union` is acceptable is when you have just produced both DataFrames with an identical, controlled schema in the same code, and even then `unionByName` costs nothing and protects you.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, trades arrive from two sources that are eventually combined: an equities feed and a derivatives feed. Both produce the same logical columns, account id, symbol, and amount, but the two teams built their DataFrames independently, and one listed amount before symbol. An engineer combined them with a positional union, and the merged report showed symbols where amounts should be and amounts where symbols should be, with no error at all. This is exactly the positional-union trap: same column count, different order, silent corruption.

This is exactly how union versus unionByName differs. A positional union blindly stacks column one on column one, so a different order scrambles the data, while unionByName matches account id to account id, symbol to symbol, and amount to amount by name, so the order no longer matters.

Problem 2 — Later a new settlement date column was added to the derivatives feed but not yet to the equities feed. A plain union now failed because the column counts differed, and the team needed the old rows to simply carry a null settlement date rather than block the pipeline. This is exactly the allow-missing-columns case: unionByName with allow missing columns produces the union of columns and fills nulls where a side lacks one.

Because a real Spark cluster is heavy, this runnable demo models a tiny schema-aware DataFrame and implements both union strategies faithfully. A `MiniFrame` carries an ordered list of column names and rows as name-to-value maps so column identity is explicit. A `PositionalUnion` combines by index and shows the corruption when orders differ. A `NameUnion` combines by column name and supports an allow-missing flag that fills nulls. The demo combines two frames with different column orders both ways to show the scramble versus the correct result, then combines frames with different column sets to show allow missing columns filling nulls.

```yaml
# application.yml
union:
  prefer-by-name: true
  allow-missing-columns: true
```

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/union-safety-demo-1.0.0.jar com.bank.union.UnionDemo

# Real PySpark:
# equities.union(derivatives)                                  # positional — risky
# equities.unionByName(derivatives)                            # by name — safe
# equities.unionByName(new_feed, allowMissingColumns=True)     # fills nulls for missing cols
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an equities frame with columns account id, symbol, amount holding one row for Rajesh, and a derivatives frame with the same logical columns but ordered account id, amount, symbol holding one row for Priya.

Step 1: The positional union checks that both frames have three columns, which they do, then appends the equities row unchanged. For the derivatives row it takes the values in the derivatives frame's own order, which is account id, then amount, then symbol, and places them into the result's columns by position, which are account id, symbol, amount. So Priya's amount lands in the symbol column and her symbol lands in the amount column.

Step 2: The demo reads Priya's row from the result and finds the symbol column holding the number eighty thousand and the amount column holding the text NIFTY future, which is the silent scramble. No error was raised because the column count matched.

Step 3: The name union takes the union of column names, which stays account id, symbol, amount since both have the same set, and for each row it copies values by column name. Priya's amount is looked up by the name amount and placed under amount, and her symbol under symbol, so the row is correct.

Step 4: The demo reads Priya's row from the name-union result and finds symbol holding NIFTY future and amount holding eighty thousand, which is correct.

Step 5: For the allow-missing case, the new feed adds a settlement date column. The name union with allow missing columns forms the union of all four columns, copies each row by name, and because the equities row has no settlement date it fills null there, while the new feed row carries its real settlement date.

Final output:

```

WARNING: union() combined by POSITION — if column orders differ, data is SCRAMBLED
WARNING: union() row for CUR3001: symbol=80000 amount=NIFTY-FUT  (SCRAMBLED!)
Oct 30, 2026 7:50:14 AM com.bank.union.NameUnion unionByName
INFO: unionByName combined by NAME (allowMissingColumns=false) — columns aligned correctly regardless of order
INFO: unionByName row for CUR3001: symbol=NIFTY-FUT amount=80000  (correct)
INFO: old equities row settlement_date = null (filled by allowMissingColumns)
INFO: new feed row settlement_date = 2026-11-01
```

  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐

  │  - columns    │ uses   │ + union(a,b)          │
  │  - rows       │        └──────────────────────┘
  │  + addRow()   │        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  + valueAt()  │◀───────│ NameUnion             │ union by name (safe)
  └──────────────┘ uses   │ + unionByName(a,b,allow)│
                          │ - appendByName()       │
                          └──────────────────────┘

  Contract for unionByName:
    Pre:  matched columns have compatible types
    Post: rows aligned by column NAME; allowMissing → union of cols, nulls filled
    Guarantee: column order differences never scramble data

  1. PositionalUnion.union(equities, derivatives)
  2.   → maps b values by index → symbol=80000 (SCRAMBLED)
  3. NameUnion.unionByName(equities, derivatives, false)

sections.s6_takeaway:
Both union and unionByName stack two DataFrames into one with all the rows of both, like a SQL union all that keeps duplicates, and the difference is purely how columns are aligned. Plain union aligns columns by position, so it combines the first column of one with the first column of the other regardless of names, checking only that the column counts match. If the two DataFrames have the same columns in a different order, union silently puts values under the wrong columns and throws no error, which is one of the nastiest silent data-corruption bugs in Spark because it passes every type check when the types happen to line up. unionByName aligns by column name, so it stacks account id on account id and amount on amount no matter the physical order, which is the alignment you actually meant.

In Spark three point one and later, unionByName also accepts allow missing columns, which lets the two sides have slightly different column sets; the result is the union of all columns and any side that lacks a column gets null for it. That is exactly what you want when schemas evolve, for example combining a legacy feed that has no settlement date with a newer feed that does, so the old rows carry null instead of the whole job failing. The reason I always prefer unionByName is correctness and resilience: pipelines change, upstream teams add columns or reorder their selects, and names are stable identifiers while positions are not, so matching by name just keeps working while matching by position quietly breaks. The nuance is that unionByName still requires compatible types and, without the allow-missing flag, still fails on differing column sets, which is desirable because it surfaces a real mismatch instead of hiding it.

At the National Bank of India this bit us when we consolidated an equities feed and a derivatives feed that had the same logical columns but were built by different teams, and one listed amount before symbol. A positional union produced a report with amounts in the symbol column and symbols in the amount column, with no error, and it took a while to notice because the schema looked fine. Switching to unionByName fixed it instantly because the columns aligned by name. Later, when the derivatives feed gained a settlement date column that the equities feed did not have, I used unionByName with allow missing columns so the old rows carried a null settlement date and the pipeline kept running. Ever since, my rule is to always union by name, often selecting a canonical column order first so the intent is visible, and to treat plain positional union as something to avoid unless I have just built both DataFrames with an identical controlled schema in the same code.
